name: Anjana (Ayurvedic collyrium)

card.summary: A traditional Ayurvedic eye preparation of herbs and minerals applied along the lash line, used for darkened, defined eyes in the manner of kohl and kajal.
card.note: Mineral-based kohl-type products can contain lead; the US FDA considers kohl unsafe.

quick.overview:
Anjana is the Ayurvedic name for a collyrium, a medicated eye application made from herbs and mineral compounds. It belongs to the same family as kohl, kajal and surma, eye cosmetics that outline and darken the eyes to make them look larger, more defined and more striking.

Ayurvedic texts describe anjana mainly as an eye treatment, and small clinical reports in Ayurvedic journals have studied formulations for eye conditions. Its cosmetic role comes from tradition: darkened lash lines framing the eye.
quick.how: Traditionally a paste or stick is drawn along the inner or outer lash line with a fine applicator. Related kajal is made from soot mixed with oil or ghee, sometimes with camphor or herbs. Ayurvedic practice also uses it in practitioner-supervised eye therapy.
quick.risks: Kohl-type products that use lead sulfide have been linked to raised blood lead, especially in children [1]. The US FDA does not list kohl as an approved color additive and considers it unsafe [1]. Eye irritation and infection from non-sterile applicators are also reported concerns.

lead: Anjana, as described in Ayurvedic texts, is a collyrium made from herbs and mineral compounds, including oxides and sulfides of antimony, zinc and lead [1]. It sits within the broader tradition of kohl, kajal and surma, which people have used to darken and define the eyes for thousands of years [1].

For appearance, the draw is a dark lash line that frames the eyes, makes them look larger and sharper, and emphasises their shape; in India, kajal is also central to classical dance makeup and is dotted on children to ward off the evil eye [1].

Ayurvedic journals publish case reports and small clinical studies on anjana formulations for eye conditions such as ulcerative keratitis and cataract [2][3]. Mineral kohls have been linked to lead exposure, so safety reports form a large part of the literature [1].

angle.text: Applied as eyeliner, anjana and its kohl and kajal relatives darken the lash line so the eyes read as larger and more defined. Herbal and soot-based versions are chosen by people who prefer traditional preparations.

paras: In Ayurveda an anjana is a medicated preparation applied to the eyes. Textbooks describe herbal and mineral forms. Kajal, the soot-based form common in South Asia, is made from soot collected from burning oil or ghee blended with oils, with camphor or sandalwood added in some recipes [1]. Surma is made from galena or other minerals [1].

Egyptians of all classes wore kohl from the Naqada III period (about 3100 BCE), originally to guard against eye ailments, and the Ebers Papyrus (about 1550 BCE) describes protective kohl compounds [1]. In India kajal is part of classical Bharatanatyam and Odissi dance makeup, and dots of kajal are applied to ward off the evil eye [1].
Darkening and outlining the eyes and emphasising their shape is the main cosmetic use; some Ethiopian and Somali women also used kohl to cleanse the eyes and to lengthen lashes [1].

Studies are small and mostly published in Ayurvedic journals. Case reports describe Ayurvedic management of ulcerative keratitis and central serous retinopathy, and small clinical studies have examined anjana formulations such as Triphaladi Ghana Vati with Elaneer Kuzhambu Anjana in immature cataract and Triyushnadi Anjana in vernal keratoconjunctivitis [2][3][4][5]. No trial has tested anjana as a cosmetic for eye appearance.

Lead-contaminated kohl has been linked to higher blood lead levels, which can cause anemia, developmental delay and, in severe cases, death; early 1990s studies found lead as high as 84% in some commercial preparations, and a later study found about a third of Egyptian and Indian samples contained lead, while some studies have disputed the link to blood lead [1]. The US FDA does not list kohl as an approved color additive and considers it unsafe [1].
